entry.title: A short history of AI, part 3: transformers and large language models (2017–2026)

link.title: A short history of AI, part 3: transformers and large language models (2017–2026)

entry.content:
Part 1 followed AI from Alan Turing to Deep Blue, and Part 2 from Deep Blue to the Transformer, the attention-based network that Google researchers proposed in June 2017. This last part covers the nine years since then. They contain more change than the previous eighty: language models grew from a research curiosity into tools used by more than a billion people, and from tools into agents that write and run code on their own. It ends with the models of late 2026, including Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon. After this, the blog turns back to the Earth for a while.

Figure 1. Milestones in AI from 2017 to 2026, discussed in this post. Rows are evenly spaced rather than drawn to scale in time. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on the sources cited below.

Pre-training: learning language by predicting words (2017–2019)

The Transformer was built for translation, but its real impact came from a different use. In 2018 OpenAI trained a Transformer on a large collection of books simply to predict the next word in a sentence, and then fine-tuned it on specific tasks; this “generative pre-training” (the GPT in ChatGPT) improved results on most of the language-understanding tasks the authors tried (Radford et al. 2018). A few months later Google’s BERT learned by filling in randomly hidden words using the context on both sides, and set new records on a wide range of benchmarks (Devlin et al. 2019).

The idea behind both is that predicting text well requires knowing a lot about the world the text describes. Nobody labels the data: the next word is its own answer, so any text on the internet becomes training material. GPT-2, trained on millions of web pages, could write passages of startling fluency and perform some tasks it had never been trained on, simply because they appeared in its training text (Radford et al. 2019).

The scaling era (2020–2022)

In January 2020 a group at OpenAI reported that the error of a language model falls as a smooth power law as the model, the data and the computing budget grow, with some trends holding over more than seven orders of magnitude (Kaplan et al. 2020). For a field used to unpredictable progress, this was a remarkable finding: it said that bigger would reliably be better, and by how much. Four months later GPT-3, with 175 billion parameters, showed what that meant in practice. Given just a few examples of a task in its prompt, without any further training, it could translate, answer questions or write simple code (Brown et al. 2020).

The race that followed is visible in Figure 2. Model size grew about 2,500-fold in five years, reaching 540 billion parameters with Google’s PaLM (Chowdhery et al. 2022). Then DeepMind showed that most of these models had been trained on too little data for their size: Chinchilla, with 70 billion parameters but four times more training text, outperformed models several times larger (Hoffmann et al. 2022). The recipe changed from “make it bigger” to “balance size and data.”

Figure 2. Number of parameters of landmark language models, as reported in the papers that introduced them. Green points are models deliberately trained on more data relative to their size. From 2023 most developers of frontier models stopped publishing model size, so the recent models cannot be plotted. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Vaswani et al. (2017), Devlin et al. (2019), Radford et al. (2019), Brown et al. (2020), Chowdhery et al. (2022), Hoffmann et al. (2022) and Touvron et al. (2023).

The empty right side of Figure 2 is itself part of the history. As language models became products, the information that would let outsiders judge them (size, training data, compute) largely disappeared from public view. The GPT-4 technical report, for example, gives no parameter count (OpenAI 2023). Since then, most of what we know about frontier models comes from benchmarks, which, as my post on vibe coding discussed, have their own problems.

From predicting text to answering people (2022–2023)

A model trained only to continue text is not an assistant. Asked a question, it may continue with more questions. The step that turned language models into assistants was fine-tuning them on human preferences: people wrote examples of good answers and ranked the model’s outputs, and the model was then trained to produce the kind of answers people preferred, a method known as reinforcement learning from human feedback. In OpenAI’s InstructGPT study, people preferred the answers of a 1.3-billion-parameter model trained this way to those of the 175-billion-parameter GPT-3 (Ouyang et al. 2022).

On 30 November 2022 OpenAI released ChatGPT, a conversational model trained with the same methods, as a free research preview (OpenAI 2022). An analyst note estimated that it reached 100 million monthly users by January 2023, which would make it the fastest-growing consumer application recorded at the time (Hu 2023). Within a year the field had changed shape:

  • GPT-4 (14 March 2023) handled images as well as text and, according to OpenAI, scored around the top 10% of test takers on a simulated bar exam (OpenAI 2023).
  • Claude, Anthropic’s first public model, was released the same day (Anthropic 2023).
  • LLaMA (February 2023) and Llama 2 (July 2023) from Meta made capable models available as open weights, and Llama 2 was free for research and commercial use (Touvron et al. 2023; Meta 2023). An ecosystem of open models grew around them.
  • Gemini (December 2023) was Google’s first model designed from the start to work with text, images, audio and video together (Google 2023).

Thinking longer, and acting (2024–2025)

Researchers had noticed that language models solve harder problems when prompted to write out their reasoning step by step, a technique called chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al. 2022). In September 2024 OpenAI’s o1 built this into training: the model was trained with reinforcement learning to produce a long internal chain of reasoning before answering, and it performed far better on mathematics and programming problems (OpenAI 2024). In January 2025 the Chinese company DeepSeek released R1, a reasoning model trained in a similar way, with its weights openly available; its Nature paper reported that the reinforcement-learning stage cost about US$294,000 in rented computing time, although that excludes the much larger cost of training the base model it started from (Guo et al. 2025). Reasoning was no longer the preserve of a few companies.

The next step was to let models act. Instead of answering a question, an agent is given a goal and tools (a terminal, a browser, a code editor) and works toward the goal over many steps, checking its own results. Anthropic released Claude Code, an agent that reads, writes and runs code in a developer’s own environment, for general use in May 2025 (Anthropic 2025), and similar tools followed from other companies. METR’s measurements, discussed in my earlier post on writing and coding with LLMs, suggest that the length of task such agents can complete on their own has been doubling every few months (Kwa et al. 2025). The vibe coding of my previous post is a direct product of this period.

AI for science, and for the Earth

The same years brought AI into the natural sciences, in ways that matter more to a hydrology lab than any chatbot. AlphaFold 2 predicted the three-dimensional structure of proteins from their amino-acid sequences with accuracy competitive with experiments, solving a problem that had been open for fifty years (Jumper et al. 2021). In 2024 the Nobel Prize in Chemistry went half to David Baker for computational protein design and half to Demis Hassabis and John Jumper for protein structure prediction, and the Nobel Prize in Physics to John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton for foundational work that enabled machine learning with artificial neural networks (Nobel Prize Outreach 2024a, 2024b).

Weather forecasting was transformed next. GraphCast, trained on decades of reanalysis data, produced ten-day global forecasts in under a minute and outperformed the world’s leading operational deterministic forecast on 90% of 1,380 verification targets (Lam et al. 2023). Its probabilistic successor GenCast beat the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts’ ensemble on about 97% of 1,320 targets (Price et al. 2025).

Hydrology moved too. A single LSTM network trained on 531 catchments at once outperformed conceptual models calibrated for each catchment individually, and learned catchment similarities that matched hydrological understanding (Kratzert et al. 2019). In 2024 Grey Nearing and colleagues showed that a global AI model could predict extreme floods in ungauged basins up to five days ahead with reliability similar to or better than the current global system’s same-day nowcasts, and the model now feeds a free public flood-warning service in more than 80 countries (Nearing et al. 2024). The question that Hsu, Gupta and Sorooshian raised in 1995, which Part 1 described, is now being asked of operational systems.

Where things stand in late 2026

The pace has not slowed. In June 2026 Anthropic released Claude Fable 5, which it described as state-of-the-art on nearly all the benchmarks it tested (Anthropic 2026a). On 22 September came Claude Opus 5.5, which Anthropic says performs at the level of its top model, Claude Fable 5.1, on most work while costing 40% less to run than Opus 5 (Anthropic 2026b). On 30 September Google announced Gemini 4 Argon, its new frontier model, reporting a state-of-the-art score on the DeepSWE software-engineering benchmark; it reached the Gemini app on 13 October (Google 2026). OpenAI’s GPT-5 family continued in parallel, and in August 2026 OpenAI described ChatGPT as having more than a billion weekly active users (OpenAI 2026).

All of these claims come from the companies themselves, and none of the models’ sizes, training data or full evaluations are public. That is the honest summary of where the story stands: the systems are more capable than ever, more widely used than any previous technology of their kind, and harder for outsiders to examine than at any point in this history.

What ninety years teach

Turing’s question has not gone away. In 1950 Turing replaced “can machines think?” with a test of behavior. Today’s models pass versions of that test daily, and the argument has moved, exactly as it did after Deep Blue, to what passing the test does and does not show.

Rules lost to learning, but not completely. The learning tradition that began with McCulloch, Pitts and Rosenblatt won decisively. Yet the most useful systems of 2026 are learned models that use rule-based tools: they call calculators, run tests and follow procedures. The two traditions of Part 1 have merged.

Data and computing power decided the timing. Almost every key idea in this series was older than the moment it worked. What changed, again and again, was the amount of data and computing power available to make it work at scale.

Measurement is the bottleneck. From the imitation game to ImageNet to today’s agent benchmarks, each era has had to invent a way to measure progress, and each measure has eventually been outgrown or gamed. For hydrologists, who have argued about model evaluation for decades, this is familiar ground, and it is where our field can contribute.

Bottom line

  • From 2018, pre-training on large amounts of text, with no labels, became the basis of language AI.
  • Scaling laws (2020) made progress predictable; models grew about 2,500-fold in five years until Chinchilla showed that data mattered as much as size.
  • Fine-tuning on human preferences turned language models into assistants; ChatGPT (2022) brought them to the public, followed by GPT-4, Claude, LLaMA and Gemini in 2023.
  • Reasoning models (2024–2025) and coding agents (2025) extended what the models can do on their own.
  • AI transformed protein science and weather forecasting and is entering operational flood forecasting; the 2024 Nobel Prizes recognized both the methods and their scientific use.
  • In late 2026 the frontier includes Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, but most of what we know about such models comes from their developers.

Questions to think about

  1. Predicting the next word turned out to require a great deal of knowledge about the world. Is predicting tomorrow’s streamflow from yesterday’s weather the same kind of problem? What would a “pre-trained” hydrological model learn?
  2. Model developers stopped publishing model sizes in 2023. What would you need to know about an AI model before trusting it in an operational flood warning system?
  3. Looking back over the three parts of this series, which idea do you think took longest to go from proposal to practical use, and why?

entry.title: A short history of AI, part 2: data, GPUs and deep learning (1997–2017)

link.title: A short history of AI, part 2: data, GPUs and deep learning (1997–2017)

entry.content:
Part 1 ended in May 1997, with IBM’s Deep Blue beating Garry Kasparov through brute-force search and hand-tuned rules. This part covers the next twenty years, in which the opposite idea won: instead of telling the machine how to solve a problem, show it enough examples and let it work out the method itself. By 2017 that approach had overtaken human performance on a standard image benchmark, mastered the game of Go without human help, and produced the network architecture behind every large language model in use today. Part 3 will pick up from there.

After Deep Blue: learning from data (1997–2006)

By the late 1990s the center of the field had moved from logic to statistics. The most successful methods of the decade were not neural networks but algorithms with solid mathematical foundations that worked well on modest data sets: support vector machines, which find the boundary between two classes that leaves the widest possible margin (Cortes & Vapnik 1995), and random forests, which average the votes of many randomized decision trees (Breiman 2001a). In the same year, the statistician Leo Breiman described a split between two “cultures”: one that starts by assuming a model of how the data were generated, and one that treats the process as unknown and judges a model only by how well it predicts (Breiman 2001b). Hydrologists will recognize the debate. It is the same tension between conceptual and data-driven models that the 1995 rainfall-runoff network in Part 1 raised.

Neural networks were out of fashion, but two ideas from this period proved decisive later. The first was the convolutional network. Yann LeCun and colleagues trained networks whose layers scan an image with small, shared filters, and used them to read handwritten digits; a check-reading system built on this approach was deployed commercially (LeCun et al. 1998). The second was memory. Ordinary recurrent networks, which process sequences one step at a time, forget quickly: the error signal used to train them shrinks with every step it is passed back through time. Sepp Hochreiter and Jürgen Schmidhuber designed the long short-term memory (LSTM) unit, a cell with gates that decide what to keep, what to add and what to forget, so that information can survive many steps (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber 1997).

Figure 1. Why LSTM networks can remember. If a signal is multiplied by a constant factor at every step, a plain recurrent network with an effective factor of 0.8 keeps almost nothing of an input from 30 steps back, while an LSTM cell whose forget gate stays open (factor 0.99) keeps most of it. The factors are chosen for illustration; in real networks they are learned and change over time. Figure by Daeha Kim; illustrative, no data.

For hydrologists, Figure 1 is more than an abstraction. A catchment’s response today depends on rain that fell weeks ago and on snow that fell months ago. A model that forgets after a few days cannot represent that memory; one with a learned, gated store can, which is why LSTM networks later became the workhorse of machine learning in hydrology.

Deep learning returns (2006–2012)

The revival began with a trick for training networks with many layers. Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues showed that a deep network could be trained one layer at a time, each layer learning to represent the output of the layer below, and then fine-tuned as a whole (Hinton et al. 2006; Hinton & Salakhutdinov 2006). The word “deep,” meaning many layers, entered the field’s vocabulary.

Two other ingredients arrived at the same time. The first was computing power from an unexpected source: graphics processing units (GPUs), built to render video games, turned out to be very good at the matrix arithmetic that neural networks need, and training on them was dramatically faster than on ordinary processors (Raina et al. 2009). The second was data. Fei-Fei Li and colleagues built ImageNet, a database of millions of photographs labeled by thousands of crowd workers according to a hierarchy of object categories (Deng et al. 2009). From 2010 its annual challenge asked programs to classify images into 1,000 categories after training on about 1.2 million labeled examples (Russakovsky et al. 2015).

Not every headline of the period came from deep learning. In 2011 IBM’s Watson won the quiz show Jeopardy! against two of its strongest champions, using a large pipeline of many different language-processing and retrieval methods rather than a single learned network (Ferrucci et al. 2010). But in speech recognition, four research groups reported in 2012 that deep neural networks had overtaken the methods that had dominated the field for decades (Hinton et al. 2012).

2012: the year the benchmark broke

The turning point came at the 2012 ImageNet challenge. A deep convolutional network built by Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Hinton, trained for several days on two consumer graphics cards, cut the top-5 error (the share of images whose correct label was not among the program’s five best guesses) to 16.4%, about ten percentage points ahead of the next-best entry (Krizhevsky et al. 2017; Russakovsky et al. 2015). The previous year’s winner had scored 25.8%. Within two years almost every competitive entry was a deep network.

Figure 2. Top-5 classification error of the winning entry in the ImageNet challenge, 2010–2017. Gray bars are methods based on hand-designed image features; blue bars are deep convolutional networks. The dashed line is the error of one trained human annotator on 1,500 test images; a second annotator with less training scored 12.0%. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Russakovsky et al. (2015), He et al. (2016) and Hu et al. (2018).

The error kept falling. In 2015 a residual network, which adds shortcut connections so that a network can be more than a hundred layers deep and still train, reached 3.57% (He et al. 2016). That was below the 5.1% measured for one carefully trained human annotator, and the result was widely reported as “superhuman.” The more careful statement is narrower: on this benchmark, with these 1,000 categories, the machine made fewer top-5 errors than one expert who had practiced for the task. A second annotator with less practice scored 12.0% (Russakovsky et al. 2015). By 2017 the winning error was 2.25%, and the challenge ended (Hu et al. 2018). The pattern will look familiar from my post on vibe coding: a public benchmark drives rapid progress, and then the meaning of the score becomes the hard question.

Learning by playing (2013–2017)

Deep networks next learned to act. DeepMind combined a convolutional network with reinforcement learning, in which a program learns from rewards rather than labeled examples, and trained a single system to play 49 Atari video games from the screen pixels and the score alone, reaching a level comparable to a professional games tester (Mnih et al. 2015).

Then came Go, a game with far too many possible positions for Deep Blue’s brute-force search. AlphaGo used two deep networks, one to suggest promising moves and one to evaluate positions, trained first on records of human games and then by playing against itself, and combined them with tree search. It beat the European champion Fan Hui 5–0 (Silver et al. 2016), and in March 2016, in Seoul, it beat Lee Sedol, one of the strongest players of the previous decade, by four games to one. For many people in Korea that match, more than any paper, marked the moment AI became real. A year later AlphaGo Zero learned the game from the rules alone, with no human games at all, and beat the version that had defeated Lee Sedol by 100 games to 0 (Silver et al. 2017).

The contrast with Part 1 is the clearest summary of these twenty years. Deep Blue’s strength came from its builders’ knowledge of chess, encoded by hand. AlphaGo Zero’s came from the rules of the game and an enormous amount of self-play.

Language: from word vectors to attention (2013–2017)

Language was harder, because meaning depends on context. A first step was to represent each word as a list of numbers learned from the contexts it appears in, so that words with similar meanings end up close together; word2vec made this fast enough to train on billions of words (Mikolov et al. 2013). Next, sequence-to-sequence models used one LSTM to read a sentence and another to write its translation (Sutskever et al. 2014). Their weakness was that the whole input sentence had to be squeezed into a single fixed-length summary. The fix, called attention, let the translating network look back at every word of the input and decide which ones mattered for the word it was writing (Bahdanau et al. 2015). In the same period, generative adversarial networks showed that two networks trained against each other could produce convincing new images (Goodfellow et al. 2014).

By 2015 the change was large enough for LeCun, Yoshua Bengio and Hinton to summarize it in a review in Nature (LeCun et al. 2015); the three later shared the 2018 Turing Award. And in June 2017 a team at Google proposed a translation model that dropped recurrence altogether and was built from attention alone. Because it processed all the words of a sentence at once rather than one at a time, it could be trained far more efficiently on GPUs. They called it the Transformer (Vaswani et al. 2017). Part 3 begins with what happened when people made it very large.

Hydrology catches up

Our field followed with a short delay. In 2018 Frederik Kratzert and colleagues showed that LSTM networks trained on daily meteorological data could simulate streamflow in hundreds of catchments in the United States with skill comparable to a well-established conceptual model, and that the network’s internal memory cells behaved in some ways like the snow and soil storages of a conceptual model (Kratzert et al. 2018). In the same year, Chaopeng Shen reviewed what deep learning could offer water resources science (Shen 2018). The question Hsu, Gupta and Sorooshian had raised in 1995, whether a network that predicts well can also teach us something, had come back in a stronger form.

What changed in twenty years

Three ingredients arrived together. The ideas behind deep learning (multilayer networks, backpropagation, convolution, LSTM) were mostly older than 2006. What changed was the arrival of large labeled data sets and cheap parallel computing, which finally made those ideas work at scale. Part 1 showed promises running ahead of data and computing power; Part 2 shows what happened when they caught up.

Learning replaced hand design, even for the inputs. Before 2012, image recognition relied on features designed by experts. After 2012, networks learned their own features from raw pixels. AlphaGo Zero took the same step for game knowledge. The trend is still running.

Benchmarks became the engine of progress, and the arguments moved with them. ImageNet focused a whole field on one number. It also showed how easily a narrow score can be read as a broad claim.

Bottom line

  • From the late 1990s, statistical learning methods replaced hand-written rules; Breiman’s “two cultures” named the split between explaining and predicting that hydrology knows well.
  • Two older ideas, convolutional networks and LSTM memory, became the building blocks of the deep-learning era.
  • Deep learning returned around 2006 and took over after 2012, when a GPU-trained network cut the ImageNet error by about ten percentage points.
  • AlphaGo (2016) and AlphaGo Zero (2017) showed that learning and self-play could beat the hand-built knowledge that powered Deep Blue.
  • Attention (2014) and the Transformer (2017) set the stage for the large language models of Part 3; hydrology adopted LSTM networks from 2018.

Questions to think about

  1. Breiman described two cultures of statistical modeling. Which one does your own research belong to, and what would you gain from the other?
  2. Why does a model of daily streamflow need memory? List the processes in a catchment that make today’s flow depend on last month’s weather.
  3. A network beat one trained human on ImageNet in 2015. What would it take for you to call a hydrological model “better than an expert hydrologist”?

entry.title: A short history of AI, part 1: from Turing to Deep Blue (1936–1997)

link.title: A short history of AI, part 1: from Turing to Deep Blue (1936–1997)

entry.content:
My recent posts have been about how to use today’s AI tools well: what they do to our writing, how to catch their errors, and when vibe coding can be trusted. Several students asked a more basic question: how did we get here? This is the first of three posts on that question. This one covers the sixty years from Alan Turing’s paper machine to the computer that beat the world chess champion (1936–1997). The second will cover the turn to data and deep learning (1997–2017), and the third the transformer and the large language models of today (2017–2026).

History is worth the detour for a practical reason. Many of the debates about AI in 2026 (whether a machine can think, whether rules or learning is the better path, how to tell real progress from hype, and how to measure intelligence at all) were first argued in the period covered here. Knowing how those arguments went the first time makes the current ones easier to judge.

Figure 1. Milestones in AI from 1936 to 1997, discussed in this post. Rows are evenly spaced rather than drawn to scale in time. The two “AI winters,” periods of reduced funding and interest, are shown with approximate dates because historians date them differently. Figure by Daeha Kim, based on the sources cited below.

A machine on paper (1936–1950)

The story usually starts with a mathematician, not a computer. In 1936 Alan Turing, then 24, wanted to answer a question in logic: is there a mechanical procedure that can decide whether any given mathematical statement is provable? To make “mechanical procedure” precise, he imagined a machine that reads and writes symbols on a tape according to a short table of rules. He then showed that a single “universal” machine could imitate any other such machine if given its rule table as input (Turing 1937). That is, in essence, the idea of the stored-program computer, described a decade before one was built.

Seven years later, the neurophysiologist Warren McCulloch and the logician Walter Pitts proposed that a nerve cell could be modeled as a simple logical unit that fires when the sum of its inputs passes a threshold, and that networks of such units could compute logical functions (McCulloch & Pitts 1943). Their paper is the ancestor of every neural network in use today.

In 1950, after his wartime codebreaking work, Turing returned to the question of thinking machines in the journal Mind. He judged the question “Can machines think?” too vague to answer, and replaced it with a game: an interrogator exchanges typed messages with a person and a machine and tries to tell which is which (Turing 1950). Turing predicted that in about fifty years a computer with a memory of about 109 bits would play the game well enough that an average interrogator would have no better than a 70% chance of identifying it correctly after five minutes of questioning. He also suggested that the most practical route to such a machine might be to build a “child machine” and educate it rather than program it directly, an idea that anticipates machine learning by decades. Turing died in 1954 and did not see the field he had imagined take shape.

Naming the field (1955–1969)

The phrase “artificial intelligence” first appeared in a funding proposal dated 31 August 1955. John McCarthy, Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester and Claude Shannon asked the Rockefeller Foundation to support a two-month summer study at Dartmouth College, based on the conjecture that every aspect of learning and intelligence could in principle be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it. They expected that a carefully chosen group working together for one summer could make a significant advance (McCarthy et al. 2006). The workshop took place in the summer of 1956. It did not produce the advance, but it gave the field its name and its founding generation.

Progress in the following years was real and quick. Allen Newell and Herbert Simon’s Logic Theorist proved theorems from Whitehead and Russell’s Principia Mathematica by searching through possible chains of reasoning (Newell & Simon 1956). Arthur Samuel’s checkers program improved by playing against itself and remembering which positions led to wins; his 1959 paper helped popularize the term “machine learning” (Samuel 1959). Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron took McCulloch and Pitts’s artificial neuron one step further: instead of having its connection weights set by hand, it adjusted them automatically from examples until it classified them correctly (Rosenblatt 1958). Rosenblatt built it in hardware, and the press coverage was enthusiastic.

The most famous program of the decade was also the simplest. Joseph Weizenbaum’s ELIZA imitated a psychotherapist by matching keywords in the user’s sentences and turning them into questions (Weizenbaum 1966). It understood nothing, and Weizenbaum said so, yet many users confided in it as if it did. He was disturbed enough by this to write a book arguing that some tasks should never be handed to computers (Weizenbaum 1976). Sixty years later, the tendency he observed, our readiness to attribute understanding to fluent text, is one of the main themes of my previous post on writing with LLMs.

Limits, and the first winter (1969–1980)

In 1969 Minsky and Seymour Papert published Perceptrons, a mathematical analysis of what a single layer of Rosenblatt-style neurons could and could not compute (Minsky & Papert 1969). The best-known limitation is easy to draw. A single perceptron separates its inputs with one straight line (or plane), so it can learn AND and OR but not XOR, which outputs 1 when exactly one of its two inputs is 1. Adding a hidden layer of neurons solves the problem, but in 1969 nobody had a practical way to train the weights of such hidden layers.

Figure 2. AND and OR can be computed by a single perceptron because one straight line separates the inputs that should give 1 from those that should give 0. For XOR no such line exists. Two hidden units, each drawing one line, solve the problem; training such hidden units became practical only in the 1980s. Figure by Daeha Kim; illustrative, no data.

The book is often blamed for a decade of neglect of neural networks. Its authors doubted that multilayer networks would do much better, but what they proved concerned single-layer ones. The wider field was in trouble too. Early programs that worked on small, clean problems failed on realistic ones, because the number of possibilities to search grows explosively with the size of the problem. In 1973 the mathematician James Lighthill, asked by the UK Science Research Council to review the field, concluded that it had failed to deliver on its promises outside a few narrow areas (Lighthill 1973). Funding in the UK was cut sharply, and in the United States military funding moved toward projects with clear applications. The period of reduced support that followed, roughly the second half of the 1970s, came to be called the first “AI winter.”

Expert systems, and the second winter (1980–1993)

AI recovered in the 1980s by narrowing its ambition. Instead of general intelligence, researchers built “expert systems” that encoded the knowledge of specialists as hundreds or thousands of if-then rules. The best-known commercial success was R1 (later called XCON), which configured orders for Digital Equipment Corporation’s VAX computers, a task that had required experienced engineers (McDermott 1982). Companies founded AI groups, specialized “LISP machines” were sold to run AI software, and in 1982 Japan launched its ambitious Fifth Generation Computer Systems project.

The boom did not last. Expert systems were brittle: they failed abruptly on cases their rules did not anticipate, and keeping thousands of rules consistent as the world changed proved expensive. Cheaper general-purpose workstations made the specialized hardware obsolete, and the market for it collapsed around 1987. The second AI winter, from the late 1980s to the early 1990s, was as much a commercial collapse as a scientific one.

Meanwhile, the neural network tradition had quietly solved its 1969 problem. In 1986 David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton and Ronald Williams showed how to train networks with hidden layers by propagating the output error backward through the network and adjusting each weight in proportion to its contribution to the error (Rumelhart et al. 1986). The method, backpropagation, had been described earlier by others, but this paper made it widely known and showed that hidden units learned useful internal representations. Multilayer networks could now learn XOR and much more.

Learning from data, and a chess match (1990s)

In the 1990s, much of AI quietly changed character. Instead of writing rules, researchers increasingly fitted statistical models to data, and judged them by how well they predicted cases they had not seen. Hydrology was an early adopter. Kuolin Hsu, Hoshin Gupta and Soroosh Sorooshian trained a three-layer neural network to simulate daily streamflow in the Leaf River basin in Mississippi and found that it represented the rainfall-runoff relationship better than both a linear time-series model and the conceptual Sacramento soil moisture accounting model. They added that, because its components had no physical meaning, it was no substitute for conceptual watershed modeling (Hsu et al. 1995). By 2000 an ASCE task committee had written a two-part review of neural networks in hydrology (ASCE Task Committee 2000). The tension they named, between models that predict well and models we can interpret, has never left our field.

The decade, and this first part of the story, ended with a symbolic victory for the older tradition. In May 1997 IBM’s Deep Blue beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov 3.5–2.5 in a six-game match. Deep Blue did not learn chess in the modern sense. Its builders credit a massively parallel computer with hundreds of special-purpose chess chips, an emphasis on deep search, a complex evaluation function and a database of grandmaster games (Campbell et al. 2002). It was a triumph of search and engineering on a problem with clear rules and a clear score, exactly the kind of problem the Dartmouth founders had in mind, forty years later than they had hoped.

What the first sixty years teach

Two traditions, both still alive. From the start there were two ideas of how to build intelligence: write down the rules (logic, search, expert systems) or let the machine learn them from examples (artificial neurons, perceptrons, backpropagation). The first dominated until the 1990s; the second dominates today. But today’s systems still combine them, for example when a language model is asked to call a calculator or run a test suite.

Promises ran ahead of data and computing power. Both winters followed periods in which researchers and funders expected general intelligence within a decade or two. The ideas were often sound; what was missing was enough data and computing power to make them work at scale. That is worth remembering whenever a forecast about AI sounds certain, in either direction.

Turing’s question is still the hard one. Turing replaced “can it think?” with “can we tell the difference?”, a test based on behavior. The benchmark debates in my recent posts are versions of the same move, and they inherit the same weakness: passing a test is not the same as having the ability the test was meant to measure.

Hydrology has been here before. The 1995 neural network that beat a conceptual model, and the authors’ caution about what it could not tell us, anticipate today’s debates about machine learning in hydrology almost exactly.

Bottom line

  • Turing defined the computer (1936) and proposed a behavioral test of machine intelligence (1950), including the idea of a machine that learns.
  • The field was named in 1955 and grew quickly, but early optimism ran into the explosion of possibilities in real problems and into the limits of single-layer perceptrons.
  • Two AI winters followed: in the late 1970s after early promises failed, and around 1987–1993 after the expert-system boom collapsed.
  • Backpropagation (1986) made multilayer neural networks trainable, and in the 1990s learning from data, including in hydrology, began to replace writing rules.
  • Deep Blue’s 1997 win was a triumph of search and engineering, not of learning, and it closed the first era.

Questions to think about

  1. Turing replaced “can machines think?” with a behavioral test. What would be a good behavioral test of whether an AI “understands” a hydrological model, and what could it miss?
  2. Why can one perceptron learn AND but not XOR? Try drawing it before looking at Figure 2.
  3. Hsu and colleagues found that a neural network predicted streamflow better than a conceptual model but warned that it was no substitute for one. Do you agree, thirty years later?

entry.title: Vibe coding, vibe writing, vibe working: what decides whether it works

link.title: Vibe coding, vibe writing, vibe working: what decides whether it works

entry.content:
In the previous post I looked at what we gain and lose when LLMs help us write and code. This one asks a narrower question that students in my group keep raising: when you hand a whole task to an AI and mostly look at the result, what decides whether the result is right? The practice has a name, vibe coding, and two newer cousins, vibe writing and vibe working. I wanted to know what the evidence says about each, and in particular how anyone measures their accuracy in a way that deserves to be called scientific.

As before, I have tried to report every number as the original authors did and to say when a source is a preprint, a company announcement or an industry report. Several of the most useful sources here are not peer-reviewed, because the field moves faster than journals do. That is itself part of the story.

Where the term came from

On 2 February 2025 Andrej Karpathy, a founding member of OpenAI and former director of AI at Tesla, posted on X about a new way of programming he called “vibe coding,” in which you “fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists” (Karpathy 2025). He described speaking his requests to an AI coding tool, accepting all of its changes without reading them and pasting error messages back without comment when something broke, and said the approach was fine for throwaway weekend projects. The post was viewed around 4.5 million times, and the term spread with unusual speed: Merriam-Webster listed it as a slang and trending entry in March 2025, and Collins English Dictionary named it Word of the Year for 2025 in November (Michels et al. 2026). Collins defines it as the use of artificial intelligence prompted by natural language to assist with the writing of computer code.

The definition that matters for this post came a few weeks after the original tweet. The programmer Simon Willison argued that using an LLM is not enough to make something vibe coding: if you have reviewed, tested and understood every line the model wrote, you are simply using it as a typing assistant (Willison 2025). Vibe coding, on this reading, is defined by not reading the code and judging it only by whether it seems to work. A recent review of the evidence adopts the same boundary (Michels et al. 2026), and so will I. The distinction is important because most of the questions below are about what happens when the human stops checking.

The other two terms came from industry. In late September 2025 Microsoft introduced an agent mode for Excel and Word and called the shift “vibe working,” with “vibe writing” as its Word-specific form: you describe the document or analysis you want and the agent plans and carries out the steps (Microsoft 2025). Nobody has yet defined these terms as carefully as Willison defined vibe coding, so I use them loosely here: handing a writing or office task to an AI and judging mainly by the result.

How accuracy is measured

There are three kinds of evidence, and they answer different questions.

Benchmarks with hidden tests. A benchmark gives a model a task and checks the result automatically. The first widely used one, HumanEval, had 164 short Python functions, each with unit tests; today’s frontier models solve almost all of them, so it no longer tells models apart. Its successor for agentic coding, SWE-bench, gives an agent a real issue from a real open-source repository and counts it as solved only if the repository’s own tests pass afterwards. Scores rose from under 2% on the original SWE-bench in late 2023 to 95% on its human-validated subset, SWE-bench Verified, by mid-2026 (Michels et al. 2026). That is the most compact summary of how fast coding capability has grown.

Randomized trials with people. Benchmarks measure the model alone. To know what happens when a person uses the model, someone has to randomly assign people to work with and without it and measure the outcome. The METR trial discussed in the previous post is the best-known example; a field experiment with 4,867 developers in three companies found 26% more completed tasks with an AI assistant (Cui et al. 2026); and a trial run by Anthropic found that developers learning a new library with AI help scored 17 percentage points lower (50% against 67%) on a test of what they had just learned (Shen & Tamkin 2026).

Telemetry and audits. Companies and researchers also measure what happens in real codebases over months: review time, bug counts, incidents and code duplication. These data are large but usually observational and often collected by vendors, so they show associations rather than causes.

Each kind has known traps, and they all push in the same direction, toward overestimating accuracy.

  • Contamination. Models may have seen the test problems during training. When OpenAI audited SWE-bench Verified in early 2026, it found that every frontier model it tested could reproduce the reference solution or verbatim details of the problem for some tasks, and among the 138 problems that its own o3 model could not solve consistently, 59.4% had defects in the tests or the problem description. It stopped reporting the benchmark in February 2026 (Michels et al. 2026).
  • Weak tests. A patch can pass the tests and still be wrong. An audit of the top 30 agents on SWE-bench found that about one in five “solved” patches was semantically incorrect but passed weak test suites (Yu et al. 2026).
  • Who runs the test. On the harder, contamination-resistant SWE-bench Pro, the best scores reported by model developers were around 80%, while the benchmark’s maintainer, running the same class of models itself, found about 59–61%, although it had not yet tested the newest models (Michels et al. 2026).

Figure 1. The same kind of system scores very differently depending on who runs the test, what counts as correct and how much of the task must work. Left: best scores on SWE-bench Verified and on the harder SWE-bench Pro, as reported by model developers and as measured independently (Michels et al. 2026). Middle: share of solutions from one agent that were functionally correct, and correct and secure (Zhao et al. 2026). Right: share of scientific coding subproblems and of whole problems solved by the best model in the published study, o1-preview, without background information (Tian et al. 2024). The three panels come from different studies and years and should not be compared with one another. Figure by Daeha Kim.

So “how accurate is vibe coding?” has no single answer. The answer depends on what is checked, by whom and how strictly. That observation turns out to be the key to the rest of this post.

What decides whether the code is right

Reading across the studies, I find eight factors with reasonably direct evidence behind them. They are not independent, and the first one runs through all the others.

1. Whether the result can be checked. The review by Michels and colleagues (2026) concludes that the decisive variable is not difficulty but verifiability. Where a mechanical check exists (a test suite, a compiler, a crash that can be reproduced), current systems are strong and improving fast, because they can try, fail and try again. Where no such check exists, failures are silent. The effect of a feedback loop is visible even in older work: letting a model run its code against unit tests and explain its own mistakes improved accuracy by up to 12% on benchmarks with unit tests, while on a text-to-SQL benchmark with no unit tests the gains were only 2–3% (Chen et al. 2024). The catch is that the model can also write the tests. AI-written tests usually compile and pass, but they detect real faults less well than human-written ones (Michels et al. 2026), because a model trying to pass its own tests writes tests that confirm its code rather than tests that could break it.

2. How completely the task is specified. Benchmarks give the model a complete, precise task. Real requests rarely are. When researchers removed key information from SWE-bench Verified issues, models were poor at noticing that anything was missing; but when they were allowed to ask the user questions, performance on the underspecified tasks improved by up to 74% over working without interaction (Vijayvargiya et al. 2025). A vague request is not a neutral starting point. The model fills the gaps with plausible assumptions, and nothing tells you which ones it chose.

3. How large and how old the codebase is. Scores drop sharply from short, self-contained tasks to long tasks in large repositories (the gap between SWE-bench Verified and Pro in Figure 1). The one independent trial that measured a slowdown studied experienced developers working in their own mature repositories (Becker et al. 2025). Michels and colleagues offer a testable conjecture for much of the disagreement in the literature, which no study has yet been designed to test: AI gains are real on new code and shrink or reverse in mature codebases, where years of undocumented decisions form a specification that cannot be checked. Long inputs are also a problem in themselves. In a controlled study of 18 models, performance became less reliable as input length grew, even on simple tasks whose difficulty was held constant (Hong et al. 2025).

4. How common the language and library are. Models are much better at languages with abundant training data. The largest public code corpus, The Stack v2, contains roughly 200 GB of Python but only about 2 GB of Julia and Fortran (Boruch-Gruszecki et al. 2025), and performance on low-resource languages such as R and Racket lags well behind Python and Java (Cassano et al. 2024). Library versions matter too: on 328 Python problems that required code compatible with a specific version of a library, the best commercial models succeeded only 48–51% of the time in the baseline setting (Misra et al. 2026). For hydrologists this is not abstract. Much of our legacy modeling code is in Fortran, and much of our analysis depends on fast-moving packages.

5. How much domain knowledge the task needs. General coding skill does not transfer automatically to scientific code. SciCode, built by scientists from 16 subfields of the natural sciences, splits 80 research problems into 338 subproblems. In the published study the best model, o1-preview, solved 28.5% of the subproblems but only 7.7% of whole problems, because every step has to be right for the whole to be right (Tian et al. 2024). Models have improved since, but the structure of the result has not changed: errors compound across steps, and a scientific workflow has many steps.

6. What “correct” means. Functional correctness is only one property. SusVibes gives agents 186 real feature requests from open-source projects for which human developers had originally committed vulnerable code. The best configuration produced functionally correct solutions 57% of the time, but only 11.8% were also secure, and adding security hints to the request did not fix this (Zhao et al. 2026). If you only check whether the code runs, you are measuring the easier of the two numbers.

7. The model and the tool around it. Model generation is the factor everyone notices, and it is real: the rise on SWE-bench from under 2% to 95% happened in about two and a half years. But the same model behaves differently depending on the harness: how many attempts it gets, whether it can run tests, which tools it can call. A benchmark score belongs to a model and its setup, and your setup is probably not the one on the leaderboard.

8. The person. In Anthropic’s trial, participants who relied heavily on the AI, by delegating the code to it or letting it debug for them, scored below 40% on the comprehension test, while those who asked conceptual questions or requested explanations alongside the code scored 65–86%, although these subgroups were very small (Shen & Tamkin 2026). The developers in the METR trial believed they were faster when they were slower (Becker et al. 2025). The person decides how well the task is specified, whether a check exists and whether anyone reads the output. Vibe coding, by definition, removes the last of these.

Put together, the factors suggest a simple rule. Vibe coding is most accurate when the task is small, well specified, in a common language and checkable by a test you trust; it is least accurate when the task is long, vague, scientific, security-sensitive or embedded in a large old codebase. Most research code in our field falls somewhere in between.

Vibe writing: how far does it go?

Writing has the same factors, but the first one, verifiability, works against it. There is no compiler for an argument and no unit test for a literature review.

Prose quality can be very high. In a preregistered study, writers trained in Master of Fine Arts programs and frontier models each wrote short passages in the style of 50 award-winning authors, and 28 expert readers and 516 general readers compared them blind. When the models were simply prompted, expert readers strongly preferred the human writing. When a model was fine-tuned on each author’s complete works, the result reversed: expert readers now preferred the AI text for both style and quality, and detectors flagged only 3% of the fine-tuned passages as machine-written, against 97% of the prompted ones (Chakrabarty et al. 2025). At the level of the sentence, AI writing can already pass for expert work.

Facts and sources are where it fails. The detector company GPTZero scanned 4,841 of the 5,290 papers accepted at NeurIPS 2025, one of the most selective AI conferences, and confirmed at least 100 fabricated citations in about 50 papers, roughly 1% of those it scanned, each of which had passed three or more reviewers (GPTZero 2026). The figure comes from a company that sells a citation checker, but the citations it lists can be checked by anyone. Tools designed for research do better but not well enough: an audit of AI search engines and deep-research agents found that a large share of their statements were not supported by the sources they themselves cited, with citation accuracy between 40% and 80% across systems (Venkit et al. 2025). Generated documentation shows the same pattern in code: early frontier models wrote inaccurate statements in about one fifth of generated code comments, and standard automatic metrics did not detect them (Michels et al. 2026).

Whole papers are possible, but rarely good ones. In 2025 Sakana AI submitted three papers written entirely by its AI Scientist system to an ICLR workshop, with the organizers’ agreement. One received an average score of 6.33, just above the acceptance threshold; the company said none of the three met its own bar for the main conference, and its internal review found citation errors (Sakana AI 2025). Later that year, Agents4Science accepted only papers with an AI as first author: of 315 submissions, 253 complete papers were reviewed by three LLM reviewers, 79 were also assessed by humans and 48 were accepted (Bianchi et al. 2025). One human reviewer, an astrophysicist, judged the papers she saw technically correct but neither interesting nor important (Hulick 2025).

And plain text is still the weak spot in office benchmarks. On GDPval tasks whose deliverable was plain text, models were rated better than professionals far less often than on tasks with spreadsheets, slides or PDFs (Patwardhan et al. 2025).

My reading is that vibe writing works for text whose value lies in its surface: a summary of a document you have read, a routine email, a first structure for a report. It fails for text whose value lies in its claims, because nothing in the process checks them. The previous post showed a second, quieter failure: even light editing shifts what the text says. A scientific paper is almost entirely claims.

Vibe working: how far does it go?

Office work sits between coding and writing: some of it has checkable outputs (a spreadsheet formula, a filled form), some does not (a recommendation, a slide narrative). The benchmarks reflect that.

Figure 2. Success rates of AI agents on benchmarks of office and freelance work. Each benchmark defines success differently (accepted by a client, all checkpoints completed, cell-level accuracy, judged at least as good as an expert’s deliverable), so the rows should not be compared with one another. The SpreadsheetBench and the December 2025 GDPval figures are reported by the companies that built the products. Figure by Daeha Kim, drawn from numbers reported in Mazeika et al. (2025), CAIS (2026), Xu et al. (2025), Microsoft (2025), Patwardhan et al. (2025) and OpenAI (2025).

  • Well-defined spreadsheet tasks. Microsoft reported that its Excel agent solved 57.2% of SpreadsheetBench tasks, against a human baseline of 71.3% (Microsoft 2025).
  • Simulated workplace. In TheAgentCompany, a simulated software company with internal websites, documents, chat and simulated colleagues, the best agent in the published version completed about 30% of 175 tasks on its own. Administrative, finance and data science tasks, which people find easy, were harder for agents than software engineering (Xu et al. 2025).
  • Expert deliverables. On GDPval, professionals with an average of 14 years of experience judged the best model’s deliverables at least as good as an expert’s in 47.6% of comparisons in the original paper (Patwardhan et al. 2025); a model released two months later was reported at 70.9% (OpenAI 2025). These are well-specified, one-shot tasks with all the necessary files provided.
  • Whole paid projects. The Remote Labor Index gives agents 240 real projects, mostly from freelance platforms, from architecture to data analysis to video, and asks whether the result would be accepted by a reasonable client as the commissioned work. At release in October 2025 the best agent succeeded on 2.5% (Mazeika et al. 2025). By mid-2026 the best model reached 15.8% (CAIS 2026): a sixfold increase in under a year, but still far from most projects.

The spread in Figure 2 is the same pattern as in Figure 1. The more the task is specified in advance and the narrower the definition of success, the higher the number. The closer the task is to a whole job, with an underspecified brief and a client who judges the result as a whole, the lower it is. One real-world example shows the cost of forgetting this. In 2024 the payment company Klarna announced that its AI assistant was doing the work of 700 customer-service agents; in 2025 its chief executive acknowledged that quality had suffered and the company began hiring people again (Michels et al. 2026).

A working rule for our group

The factors above can be turned into a few questions to ask before handing a task to an AI and judging it by the result.

  • Can I check the result with something I trust and did not let the model write? A water balance that must close, an analytical solution, a published benchmark catchment, a table I can recompute by hand. If yes, vibe away and run the check. If no, read the output as if a new student wrote it.
  • Have I said everything the task needs? Ask the model to list its assumptions or ask you questions before it starts. The evidence says it will not do this on its own, and it helps a great deal when it does.
  • Is the task in familiar territory for the model? Python and common packages are; old Fortran code, a specific library version or a specialized hydrological model are less so.
  • How long is the chain of steps? Errors compound. Break long work into pieces you can check one at a time.
  • Is “it runs” the right definition of correct? For anything that handles files, credentials, other people’s data or design decisions, it is not.
  • Is the value of the output in its claims? If so, as in a paper, a proposal or a report, every claim and every reference needs a source you have opened.
  • Am I learning this skill right now? If so, ask for explanations, not answers.

Bottom line

  • “Vibe coding” was coined by Andrej Karpathy on 2 February 2025 and was Collins Word of the Year for 2025. What defines it is not using an AI but not reading what the AI wrote. “Vibe writing” and “vibe working” were introduced by Microsoft in September 2025.
  • Its accuracy is measured with benchmarks, randomized trials and field data. All three tend to overestimate it, through contamination, weak tests and self-reporting.
  • The decisive factor is whether the result can be checked. Specification, codebase size and age, language and library, domain knowledge, the definition of correctness, the tool setup and the person all matter as well.
  • Vibe writing produces prose that can pass for expert work, but fabricated citations and unsupported claims are common, and nothing in the process catches them.
  • Vibe working succeeds on well-defined tasks and mostly fails on whole projects, though that is changing quickly.
  • The narrower and more checkable the task, the more you can trust the vibes. For research, that usually means building the check first.

Questions to think about

  1. For the last piece of code an AI wrote for you, what was the check that told you it was right? Did the AI write that check?
  2. Take one routine task in your research and write down everything the AI would need to know to do it correctly. How much of that would you normally leave unsaid?
  3. Which parts of a scientific paper could you check mechanically, and which could only be checked by reading the sources? What does that imply for how you use AI to write?

한 줄 요약 (Korean summary). “바이브 코딩”은 안드레이 카파시가 2025년 2월 2일 X에 올린 글에서 처음 쓴 말로, 코드가 존재한다는 사실조차 잊고 AI에 맡기는 방식을 가리키며, 콜린스 사전의 2025년 올해의 단어로 뽑혔다. 핵심은 AI를 쓰는 것이 아니라 AI가 쓴 코드를 읽지 않는다는 데 있다. “바이브 라이팅”과 “바이브 워킹”은 2025년 9월 마이크로소프트가 엑셀·워드 에이전트를 내놓으며 붙인 이름이다. 정확도는 숨겨진 테스트가 있는 벤치마크, 사람을 무작위로 배정한 실험, 실제 현장 데이터로 측정하지만, 학습 데이터 오염, 허술한 테스트, 개발사 자체 보고 때문에 대체로 과대평가된다. 예를 들어 SWE-bench Verified에서는 95%까지 올랐지만 더 어려운 SWE-bench Pro를 독립 기관이 직접 돌리면 약 60%였고, 기능상 맞는 코드가 57%여도 보안까지 갖춘 코드는 11.8%에 그쳤다. 정확도를 가르는 가장 큰 요인은 결과를 기계적으로 검증할 수 있는가이며, 과제를 얼마나 완전하게 명시했는가(질문을 허용하면 최대 74% 향상), 코드베이스의 크기와 연식, 언어와 라이브러리의 흔한 정도, 필요한 전문 지식(과학 코딩 문제 전체 정답률 7.7%), “정답”의 정의, 도구 환경, 그리고 사람이 함께 작용한다. 바이브 라이팅은 전문가 수준으로 읽히는 문장을 만들 수 있지만(작가별로 미세조정한 모델의 글을 전문가 독자가 더 선호), 가짜 인용과 근거 없는 주장을 걸러 주는 장치가 없다(NeurIPS 2025 채택 논문의 약 1%에서 가짜 인용 확인, 딥리서치 도구의 인용 정확도 40–80%). 바이브 워킹은 잘 정의된 과제에서는 상당히 잘하지만(스프레드시트 57.2%, 사람 71.3%) 실제 유료 프리랜서 프로젝트 전체를 맡기면 대부분 실패한다(2025년 10월 2.5%에서 2026년 15.8%로 빠르게 상승 중). 결국 과제가 좁고 검증 가능할수록 맡겨도 되고, 연구에서는 AI에게 일을 맡기기 전에 믿을 수 있는 검증 기준부터 직접 만들어야 한다.
